# Step 20: closed tensor curvature estimate using `E = Ric + g`

## 1. Purpose of this step

The Step 19 Whitney reduction removes the cutoff-level degeneracy of
`partial_t - chi^2 Delta`, but the previous two-field formulation treated
`E = Ric + g` and `Rm` as if their gradients were independent.  They are not.
On every smooth time-slice of the cutoff flow

\[
  \partial_t g=-2aE,\qquad a=\chi^2,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,
\]

one has, in an orthonormal frame,

\[
  E_{ij}=R_{kikj}+g_{ij},\qquad
  \nabla_pE_{ij}=\nabla_pR_{kikj}.
\]

Thus

\[
  |\nabla E|\le C_4|\nabla \operatorname{Rm}|,
  \qquad |E|\le C_4(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}.
\]

These identities are geometric contractions.  They do not require the initial
near-Einstein pointwise bound to persist.  Their main use is in the Hessian
cutoff terms: after integrating `nabla^2 a` by parts, every `nabla E` term can
be absorbed by the same full curvature dissipation as `nabla Rm`.  This replaces
the separate high-power defect-gradient energy from Step 19 by a closed
curvature-power inequality.

This does **not** control the unweighted defect energy by itself.  The global
quantity

\[
  Q(t)=\int_M|E(t)|^2\,d\mu_t
\]

is still separate because `aE` gives no pointwise control where `a` is small.
Section 7 records the corrected triangular estimate needed for `Q`.

## 2. Index-level variation and the absence of an Einstein-independent source

Use the standard variation formula for the `(0,4)` curvature tensor.  If
`h = partial_t g`, then schematically

\[
\begin{aligned}
(\partial_t R)_{ijkl}
=&\frac12\{\nabla_i\nabla_k h_{jl}+\nabla_j\nabla_l h_{ik}
        -\nabla_i\nabla_l h_{jk}-\nabla_j\nabla_k h_{il}\}\\
&+ h*R .
\end{aligned}
\]

For the normalized cutoff flow, `h=-2aE`.  Expanding second derivatives gives

\[
  \nabla\nabla(aE)=a\nabla\nabla E
        +(\nabla a)*\nabla E+(\nabla^2a)*E .       \tag{2.1}
\]

The first term supplies the principal curvature Laplacian after applying the
Bianchi identities and commuting derivatives.  The algebraic curvature terms
also receive contributions from the `h*R` part of the variation.  The resulting
structure is

\[
  a\nabla\nabla E+h*R
  = a\Delta \operatorname{Rm}+a(\operatorname{Rm}*\operatorname{Rm})
    +a(E*\operatorname{Rm})+a\operatorname{Rm},   \tag{2.2}
\]

up to the usual sign and tensor-type conventions.  The linear `a Rm` term is
therefore not attributed solely to `a nabla nabla E`; it is part of the algebraic
variation, including the normalized-flow contribution.  It is harmless in power
energies because `a<=1` and it is lower than the quadratic reaction after using
`F=(1+|Rm|^2)^{1/2}`.

The important point is that (2.1) has no term depending only on `nabla^2 a` and
`g`.  Splitting `-2aE` as `-2a Ric -2a g` creates artificial Hessian pieces, but
in the full variation they recombine into `(nabla^2 a)*E`.  Therefore an exact
negative Einstein metric, for which `E=0`, is stationary even in the transition
where `nabla a` and `nabla^2 a` are nonzero.

## 3. Power energy with the regularized curvature norm

Set

\[
  H=\operatorname{Rm},\qquad F=(1+|H|^2)^{1/2},\qquad q\ge2,
\]

and let `eta` be a spatial cutoff supported in one Whitney ball
`B_ell(y)`, with

\[
  \ell=c r\chi_0,
  \qquad \chi_0=\chi(y)>0,
  \qquad a_0=\chi_0^2 .
\]

On this ball, the Step 19 Whitney bounds give

\[
  (1-Lc)^2a_0\le a\le (1+Lc)^2a_0,
\]

and

\[
  \frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}=4|\nabla\chi|^2\le 4L^2r^{-2},
  \qquad
  a|\nabla\eta|^2\lesssim c^{-2}r^{-2}.          \tag{3.1}
\]

Test the curvature equation against `eta^2 F^(q-2) H`, including the metric and
volume variations.  The principal `a Delta H` term gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
q\int\eta^2F^{q-2}\langle H,a\Delta H\rangle
\le&-c q\int\eta^2aF^{q-2}|\nabla H|^2 \\
&+Cq\int a|\nabla\eta|^2F^q
 +Cq\int\eta^2\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}F^q .       \tag{3.2}
\end{aligned}
\]

The last term in (3.2) is one of the regular first-derivative cutoff remainders.
The variable coefficient does not create an inverse power of `chi` because of
(3.1).

The quadratic curvature reaction, the normalized `aH` term, norm variation and
volume variation have the schematic bound

\[
  Cq\int\eta^2 a F^{q+1}+Cq\int\eta^2 aF^q .     \tag{3.3}
\]

## 4. Hessian-cutoff terms close with curvature dissipation

A representative Hessian term is

\[
  I=q\int\eta^2F^{q-2}\,H*(\nabla^2a)*E .        \tag{4.1}
\]

Integrating by parts once,

\[
\begin{aligned}
I=&-q\int \nabla a * \nabla(\eta^2F^{q-2}H*E) \\
=&-q\int\eta^2\nabla a*F^{q-2}(\nabla H)*E
  -q\int\eta^2\nabla a*F^{q-2}H*(\nabla E)       \\
&-q(q-2)\int\eta^2\nabla a*F^{q-3}(\nabla F)*H*E
  -2q\int\eta\nabla\eta*\nabla a*F^{q-2}H*E .   \tag{4.2}
\end{aligned}
\]

Using

\[
  |E|\le C_4F,
  \qquad |\nabla E|\le C_4|\nabla H|,
  \qquad |\nabla F|\le |\nabla H|,
\]

every nonlocalization term in (4.2) is bounded by

\[
  Cq^2\int\eta^2|\nabla a|F^{q-1}|\nabla H|.
\]

Young's inequality gives, for any small `epsilon`,

\[
\begin{aligned}
|I|\le& \epsilon q\int\eta^2aF^{q-2}|\nabla H|^2 \\
&+C_\epsilon q^3\int\eta^2\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}F^q
 +Cq\int a|\nabla\eta|^2F^q .                  \tag{4.3}
\end{aligned}
\]

The direct `(nabla a)*nabla E` terms from (2.1) satisfy the same bound, again
because `nabla E` is a contraction of `nabla H`.

Thus the Hessian cutoff has been removed in the weak energy sense without
introducing a separate high-power defect-gradient energy.  What remains is a
larger `q`-dependent coefficient in the regular cutoff potential
`(|nabla a|^2/a)F^q`.

## 5. Closed curvature-power inequality on one Whitney ball

Combining (3.2), (3.3), and (4.3), and absorbing a small portion of the gradient
term, yields

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\int\eta^2F^q
&+c q\int\eta^2aF^{q-2}|\nabla H|^2 \\
&\le C q\int\eta^2aF^{q+1} \\
&\quad + C q^3\int\eta^2\left(\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}+a\right)F^q
      +C q\int a|\nabla\eta|^2F^q .             \tag{5.1}
\end{aligned}}
\]

The exact powers of `q` can be improved by a more careful tensor calculation,
but (5.1) is enough to reveal the structure:

* it is closed in curvature;
* it contains no term `a|nabla E|^2 F^(q-2)`;
* it contains no inverse power of `chi`;
* all cutoff contributions are measured by `r^{-2}` and `c^{-2}r^{-2}` on a
  Whitney ball.

The execution script

`workspace/scripts/step20_tensor_closed_curvature_energy.py`

records the same term ledger and the exponent bookkeeping.

## 6. Consequence for pointwise curvature: finite exponent before mean value

In dimension four the reaction term in (5.1) is controlled by the critical
Sobolev product.  With `phi=eta F^(q/2)`,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int\eta^2 aF^{q+1}
&\lesssim a_0\|F\|_{L^2(B_\ell)}\|\eta F^{q/2}\|_{L^4(B_\ell)}^2 \\
&\le \beta_\ell
\left(\int a|\nabla(\eta F^{q/2})|^2
      +\ell^{-2}\int a\eta^2F^q\right),          \tag{6.1}
\end{aligned}
\]

where the Step 19/A03 cancellation gives

\[
  \beta_\ell=S_\ell\|F\|_{L^2(B_\ell)}
   \le C\sqrt{1+K_0}\,r^2,
  \qquad\text{independent of }\chi_0\text{ and collapsed volume.}       \tag{6.2}
\]

The additional `1` comes from the regularized norm `F=(1+|Rm|^2)^{1/2}`: the
constant part contributes `S_ell Vol(B_ell)^{1/2} <= C ell^2 <= C r^2`.

Absorbing (6.1) into the gradient term in (5.1) requires smallness of the form

\[
  C(q)\beta_\ell<c .                              \tag{6.3}
\]

The script table shows the important feature: in a direct power iteration the
threshold worsens with `q`.  Therefore the Whitney scaling by itself should not
be read as an all-exponent Li iteration.  A better route is:

1. use (5.1), time integration, and critical smallness to create at positive
   time one fixed exponent `q_0>2`, for instance `q_0=3` or `q_0=4`, without
   assuming such an initial `L^{q_0}` bound;
2. use this supercritical curvature integrability on nested positive-time
   Whitney cylinders to run a De Giorgi/Moser mean-value argument in which the
   potential is now spatially supercritical;
3. only then derive a pointwise estimate of the form

\[
   |a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t
\]

or an integrated substitute strong enough for the later defect estimate.

Failure of all-exponent critical absorption would not invalidate the Whitney
approach; it would only select this finite-exponent-plus-mean-value route.

## 7. Correct triangular estimate for unweighted defect energy

The previous Step 19 note inherited an unsafe inference.  An inequality of the
form

\[
  Q'(t)\le C r^{-2}Q(t)+\varepsilon X(t),
  \qquad X(t)=\int a|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|^2,
\]

does **not** imply `Q(T) <= C Q(0)` at fixed smoothing scale, because
`int_0^T X(t)dt` may be `O(A)` in the LeBrun sequence.  This would leave an
`O(epsilon A)` error, not `o(A)`.

The correct defect estimate must use the triangular structure of the flow.  Since
`h=-2aE`, the equation for `E` has no curvature-only source:

\[
  \partial_tE=a\Delta_LE-2aE+(\nabla a)*\nabla E+(\nabla^2a)*E
             +a(\operatorname{Rm}*E)+a(E*E).      \tag{7.1}
\]

Testing by `eta^2E` and integrating the Hessian cutoff term by parts gives

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\int\eta^2|E|^2
&+c\int\eta^2a|\nabla E|^2 \\
&\le C\int\eta^2\left(\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}+a+a|\operatorname{Rm}|\right)|E|^2
   +C\int a|\nabla\eta|^2|E|^2 .                \tag{7.2}
\end{aligned}}
\]

The algebraic curvature and quadratic-defect terms are potentials multiplying
`E^2`; using `|E| <= C F`, they are bounded by `C a(1+|Rm|)|E|^2`.  In dimension
four the curvature part is absorbed exactly as in the curvature estimate:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|\,|\eta E|^2
&=\int |\operatorname{Rm}|\,|\chi\eta E|^2 \\
&\le \|\operatorname{Rm}\|_2\,\|\chi\eta E\|_4^2 \\
&\le \beta_\ell\left(\int\eta^2a|\nabla E|^2
      +r^{-2}\int\eta^2|E|^2\right).            \tag{7.3}
\end{aligned}
\]

For sufficiently small `beta_ell`, (7.2)--(7.3) yield the finite-neighbor system

\[
  \frac{d}{dt}Q_\alpha(t)
     \le C(c,L,N)r^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}Q_\beta(t).  \tag{7.4}
\]

Summing unnormalized local energies over a bounded-overlap family gives

\[
  Q_{\mathrm{support}}(T)
     \le \exp(C_NT/r^2)Q_{\mathrm{support}}(0).  \tag{7.5}
\]

Outside the support, `a=0` and the metric is stationary.  Therefore (7.5), not an
additive `epsilon X` inequality, is the route that can preserve
`Q(T)/A -> 0` from `Q(0)/A -> 0`.

The execution script

`workspace/scripts/step20_triangular_defect_energy.py`

records this correction and shows numerically why the discarded additive form is
insufficient at the scale of the LeBrun topology parameter.

## 8. Revised PDE targets after this step

The Step 19 pair of targets should be reformulated.

**Curvature target.**  Prove a localized Whitney-cylinder estimate from (5.1):
small critical `L^2` curvature energy gives either

\[
  |a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t,
\]

or first gives a fixed supercritical `L^{q_0}` bound strong enough to obtain the
same pointwise bound by a positive-time mean-value argument.  The constants must
be independent of `chi_0` and collapsed volume, while their dependence on the
fixed exponent is allowed.

**Derivative target.**  If a later Bernstein estimate is still needed, derive it
from the curvature-controlled equation for `U=aE`.  A03's `p>4` threshold remains
relevant for connection and cutoff-Hessian drift, but the high-power
curvature estimate itself no longer needs a separate defect-gradient energy.

**Unweighted defect target.**  Prove the triangular local and support-summed
estimate (7.2)--(7.5).  This is the only form currently capable of preserving
`Q/A -> 0` at a fixed smoothing scale.

This step therefore changes the analytic structure: the curvature-power layer is
more closed than the two-field Step 19 description, while direct all-exponent
critical iteration is less secure than the Step 19 wording suggested.  The
central unfinished work is now a rigorous localized parabolic theorem based on
(5.1), plus the triangular defect estimate (7.5).  The broader Yau 26 problem
remains open; this is still only the critical four-dimensional negative
LeBrun/Ishida-LeBrun laboratory.

## 9. TTCS verification and repairs incorporated

TTCS independently supported the main Step 20 change: because all contractions
and covariant derivatives are taken with respect to the current metric, `nabla E`
is controlled by `nabla Rm`, and high-power curvature energies can close without
separate high-power defect-gradient energies.  It also supported the triangular
unweighted defect estimate as the correct replacement for the old additive
`epsilon X` inference.

The verification required several repairs, now inserted above:

1. The linear `a Rm` term in the curvature equation should not be attributed
   solely to `a nabla nabla E`; it also comes from the algebraic `h*Rm` part of
   the curvature variation.
2. The schematic `E` equation should not contain a stray `(nabla a)*Rm*E` term.
   The curvature terms are `a Rm*E` (as part of, or adjacent to, `a Delta_L E`)
   and `a E*E`, so (7.2) has the potential `a(1+|Rm|)|E|^2`.
3. Since `F=(1+|Rm|^2)^{1/2}`, the Whitney Sobolev product is
   `S_ell ||F||_2 <= C sqrt(1+K0) r^2`; the constant part contributes `O(r^2)`.
4. A fixed `L^{q0}` input at `t=0` is not available from critical `L^2`; the
   finite-exponent route must create such integrability at positive time, as in
   Li's proof where local `L^2` persistence yields an `L^3` potential before a
   linear Moser step.
5. Final constants still depend on the tensor type, evolving metric comparison,
   local support budget, Whitney neighbor count, cutoff constants, and precise
   `q` bookkeeping.  No pointwise `|a Rm| <= C/t` theorem has yet been proved.

The additional script `workspace/scripts/step20_finite_exponent_route.py` records
this finite-exponent logic.  It shows schematically that unlimited critical
absorption would require a threshold deteriorating with `q`, while reaching a
single exponent such as `q0=3` or `4` remains compatible with fixed small beta and

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Step 20: finite-exponent route after the closed curvature-power inequality.

This script models the exponent bookkeeping suggested by Li's Theorem 3.4 proof:
critical L^2 smallness is used to keep local L^2 energy small and obtain a
positive-time L^3 curvature potential, rather than to absorb a reaction at every
unbounded exponent.  It is a bookkeeping model, not a PDE proof.
"""
import math

print("="*78)
print("FINITE-EXPONENT ROUTE BOOKKEEPING")
print("="*78)
print("Li source lines 245-255: after local L2 persistence, the proof derives")
print("  int_{B_r} f^3 <= C A e0^3 t^{-1}")
print("then applies a linear Moser theorem.  This is finite-exponent, not an")
print("all-exponent critical absorption at t=0.")

# Symbols normalized to Whitney radius/time.
# Let e0 = ||F||_2 on a Whitney ball, A2 = squared Sobolev coefficient S.
# beta = S e0.  The Li L3 potential scale is mu^3 ~ S e0^3 / t.
for beta in [0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001]:
    print(f"\nAssume beta=S||F||_2 = {beta:g}")
    for tau in [1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1]:
        # normalized time tau = t/r^2.  Potential coefficient for L^3 scales beta*e0^2/t,
        # but e0 is hidden in beta; we display the t^{-1} singularity and beta dependence.
        mu_scale = beta / tau
        print(f"  tau={tau:7.1e}: finite L3 potential scale ~ beta/tau = {mu_scale:8.3e}")

print("\nDirect all-exponent route would need beta < const/q at each exponent q:")
for beta in [0.02, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001]:
    qmax = 1.0/(20.0*beta)  # schematic from previous script C=20
    print(f"  beta={beta:g}: schematic direct absorption stops near q ~ {qmax:.1f}")

print("\nInterpretation:")
print("  - Critical smallness can plausibly create one positive-time L3 (or fixed q0>2) bound.")
print("  - It should not be assumed to run an unlimited q-doubling iteration with the same beta.")
print("  - The missing theorem is a localized Li/Wang mean-value step using the finite")
print("    supercritical curvature potential on nested Whitney cylinders.")
print("PASS")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Step 20: algebraic ledger for the closed curvature-power estimate under

    d_t g = -2 a E,  a = chi^2,  E = Ric + g,

using the identities E = contraction(Rm) + g and nabla E = contraction(nabla Rm).

This script does not prove a PDE theorem.  It checks the exponent bookkeeping in
one localized tensor-energy calculation after the Hess(a) terms are integrated
by parts and all nabla E terms are absorbed into the full tensor curvature
dissipation rather than a separate defect-gradient energy.
"""
from fractions import Fraction
import math

# Dimension four constants are represented schematically.
n = 4

# Choose harmless schematic constants so the numerical thresholds are transparent.
# The important output is q-dependence, not the particular constants.
C_nablaE = math.sqrt(n)        # |nabla Ric| <= sqrt(n)|nabla Rm| for a contraction in an ON frame
C_E = math.sqrt(n + 1)         # |Ric+g| <= C_E*(1+|Rm|^2)^1/2, schematic safe constant
C_reaction = 20.0             # schematic tensor reaction constant
C_cut = 16.0                  # schematic cutoff-commutator constant
c_diff = 1.0                  # normalized coefficient in front of a F^(q-2)|nabla Rm|^2

print("="*78)
print("STEP 20 CLOSED CURVATURE-POWER LEDGER")
print("="*78)
print("Flow: d_t g = -2 a E, a=chi^2, E=Ric+g")
print("F=(1+|Rm|^2)^(1/2), test tensor equation against eta^2 F^(q-2) Rm")
print()
print("Geometric substitutions used on every smooth flow time:")
print(f"  |nabla E| <= C4 |nabla Rm|, with schematic C4={C_nablaE:.3f}")
print(f"  |E| <= C4 F, with schematic C4={C_E:.3f}")
print("These do not use the initial pointwise smallness of E.")

print("\nTerm ledger after expanding nabla^2(aE):")
ledger = [
    ("a*nabla^2 E", "principal a*Delta Rm + a*Rm*Rm + a*Rm"),
    ("nabla a * nabla E", "<= eps*a*F^(q-2)|nabla Rm|^2 + C eps^-1 |da|^2/a F^q"),
    ("nabla^2 a * E", "integrate by parts -> nabla a*nabla E, nabla a*E*nabla Rm, eta-gradient"),
    ("a*E*Rm", "<= C a F^(q+1)"),
    ("norm/volume variation", "<= C a F^(q+1) + C a F^q"),
]
for t, reduction in ledger:
    print(f"  {t:24s} -> {reduction}")

print("\nRepresentative Hess(a) integration by parts:")
print("  I = int eta^2 F^(q-2) Rm * Hess(a) * E")
print("  I = -int nabla a * nabla(eta^2 F^(q-2) Rm * E)")
print("    terms with nabla E are bounded by nabla Rm; no separate nabla E energy is needed.")
print("  Young gives C q^2 int eta^2 |da|^2/a F^q + C int a|nabla eta|^2 F^q")

print("\nClosed local inequality produced by the ledger:")
print("  d/dt int eta^2 F^q + c_q int eta^2 a F^(q-2)|nabla Rm|^2")
print("    <= C q int eta^2 a F^(q+1)")
print("       + C q^2 int eta^2 ( |da|^2/a + a + a|nabla eta|^2 ) F^q")
print("       + C q^2 int a|nabla eta|^2 F^q")
print("where |da|^2/a = 4|dchi|^2 and no inverse power of chi appears.")

# Direct critical absorption threshold for the term int a F^(q+1):
# In dimension 4, Sobolev gives int a F^(q+1) <= beta * (D_q + ell^-2 Y_q).
# Reaction coefficient is schematic C_reaction*q while diffusion coefficient is c_diff*(q-1)/q ~ 1.
print("\nDirect critical absorption threshold versus exponent:")
print("  Assume int a F^(q+1) <= beta*(D_q + ell^-2 Y_q).")
print("  Need C*q*beta < c to absorb into D_q.")
print("  This table illustrates why a direct all-exponent iteration is not automatic.")
print("    q        beta_max=c/(C*q)")
for q in [2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 32, 64, 128]:
    beta_max = c_diff/(C_reaction*q)
    print(f"  {q:4d}      {beta_max:10.4e}")

# Fixed-exponent route: choose q0 and use supercritical exponent p=q0?  For curvature in 4D, p>2.
print("\nFixed-exponent alternative:")
for q0 in [Fraction(5,2), Fraction(3,1), Fraction(4,1), Fraction(6,1)]:
    beta_max = c_diff/(C_reaction*float(q0))
    supercritical = float(q0) > 2.0
    print(f"  q0={q0}: beta threshold ~ {beta_max:.4e}, spatial exponent >2? {supercritical}")
print("Reaching one finite q0>2 is compatible with fixed small beta; a later mean-value")
print("argument can use F as a supercritical curvature potential instead of absorbing")
print("critical energy at unbounded q.")

# Cutoff derivative sizes on a Whitney ball ell=c*r*chi0.
print("\nWhitney coefficient normalization:")
print("  ell=c*r*chi0, a0=chi0^2, |dchi|<=L/r")
print("  a|d eta|^2 ~ a0/ell^2 = 1/(c^2 r^2)")
print("  |da|^2/a = 4|dchi|^2 <= 4L^2/r^2")
print("Both are independent of chi0; only the constants c^{-2}, L^2 remain.")

print("\nPASS: exponent ledger supports a closed curvature-only power inequality;")
print("      it also shows direct all-exponent absorption needs further argument,")
print("      while a finite supercritical exponent route remains viable.")

# Route assessment after Step 20

## What changed

Step 20 tested the structural simplification suggested by the Strategist:
`E=Ric+g` is a contraction of curvature plus the metric, and `nabla E` is a
contraction of `nabla Rm`.  This changes the analytical target for the Whitney
cutoff flow.

## Established in this step

1. **Closed curvature-power ledger.**  For

   `partial_t g = -2 chi^2 (Ric+g)`, `a=chi^2`, `F=(1+|Rm|^2)^(1/2)`, testing
   against `eta^2 F^(q-2) Rm` gives after integrating Hess(a) by parts:

   `d/dt int eta^2 F^q + c q int eta^2 a F^(q-2)|nabla Rm|^2`

   `<= C q int eta^2 a F^(q+1) + C q^3 int eta^2(|da|^2/a + a)F^q + C q int a|nabla eta|^2 F^q`.

   The terms with `nabla E` close because `|nabla E| <= C|nabla Rm|`; no separate
   high-power defect-gradient energy is needed for the curvature layer.  TTCS
   added two repairs now incorporated in the note: the linear `a Rm` term belongs
   to the algebraic curvature variation rather than solely to `a nabla^2E`, and
   the regularized norm gives `beta <= C sqrt(1+K0) r^2`.  The script
   `workspace/scripts/step20_tensor_closed_curvature_energy.py` records the term
   ledger and exponent bookkeeping.

2. **Direct all-exponent critical absorption remains unproved.**  The reaction
   term can be absorbed using the 4D Sobolev product `beta <= C sqrt(1+K0) r^2`,
   but the threshold worsens with the exponent.  The better route is to create
   one finite exponent `q0>2` at positive time and then use a mean-value argument
   with a supercritical curvature potential.

3. **Correct triangular defect estimate.**  The inherited Step 19 sentence
   that `Q(T)<=C Q(0)` follows from an inequality containing `+epsilon X` was
   repaired.  At fixed smoothing scale an `O(A)` integral of `X` would leave an
   `O(epsilon A)` error, not `o(A)`.  The valid form must use the homogeneous
   equation for `E`: after integrating Hess(a) by parts, curvature appears as
   `a|Rm||E|^2` (the earlier stray `(nabla a)*Rm*E` term is removed) and can be
   absorbed into defect dissipation by the same 4D Sobolev product.  The resulting
   finite-neighbor inequality is

   `dQ_alpha/dt <= C r^{-2} sum_{beta~alpha} Q_beta`, hence
   `Q_support(theta r^2) <= exp(C theta) Q_support(0)`.

   The script `workspace/scripts/step20_triangular_defect_energy.py` records this
   and illustrates why the additive form fails to preserve `Q/A -> 0`.

4. **Patched inherited note.**  `workspace/notes/step19_whitney_tensor_estimate.md`
   now points to the Step 20 replacement for the unweighted defect estimate and
   for the all-exponent iteration wording.

## Current mathematical state

The Whitney reduction remains valuable: cutoff-level degeneracy and collapsed
volume still cancel on each adapted ball.  Step 20 improves the tensor structure:
the curvature regularity layer can be studied as one closed curvature equation,
not as a full two-field high-power system.  The remaining hard PDE problem is
more precise:

- prove the localized power inequality rigorously with all curvature variation
  contractions and evolving-measure terms;
- use it to create a fixed supercritical curvature exponent at positive time on
  Whitney cylinders, without assuming such initial data;
- derive the pointwise weighted curvature bound or an equivalent positive-time
  mean-value estimate;
- prove the triangular support-summed defect estimate for `Q/A -> 0`.

A03's `p>4` Bernstein threshold remains relevant for controlling connection and
cutoff-Hessian drift if the later first-exit argument needs those derivative
bounds, but it is no longer needed as a separate high-power input for the
curvature energy itself.

## Best next work

Agent2 should turn the Step 20 ledger into a rigorous local proposition: write
index contractions for the curvature variation under `h=-2aE`, prove the
inequality for `F^q`, and choose a fixed exponent `q0` for which the 4D Sobolev
absorption is feasible.  In parallel or afterward, Agent3 should test the
finite-exponent-plus-mean-value route by implementing a model parabolic iteration
with q-dependent constants to see what time/exponent regime is plausible.  The
unweighted `Q` estimate should be developed from the triangular identity, not
from any additive curvature-dissipation remainder.

This still addresses only the critical four-dimensional negative
LeBrun/Ishida-LeBrun laboratory.  The full Yau 26 proposition, positive branch,
higher dimensions, and Lean formalization remain open.

## TTCS verification update

TTCS verified the main structural simplification but sharpened the theorem target.
The `E` equation must not contain a `(nabla a)*Rm*E` term; curvature enters as the
potential `a Rm*E` (and `aE*E`) so the unweighted defect estimate remains
triangular.  The regularized norm changes the Sobolev product to
`C sqrt(1+K0) r^2`.  The finite-exponent route cannot assume initial `L^{q0}`;
it must create a positive-time `L^3` or fixed `L^{q0}` estimate from local `L^2`
persistence, following the pattern of Li source lines 245-255.  New script:
`workspace/scripts/step20_finite_exponent_route.py`.

# Step 21: Conditional finite-exponent smoothing lemma

> **STEP 22 ENERGY CORRECTION.** The finite-exponent conclusion in this note is
> stronger than its hypotheses support.  The available input on a support
> component is `int_U F^2 <= M Vol(U)`.  For a Whitney ball
> `W=B_ell(y)`, Bishop--Gromov gives only
> `ell^4 fint_W F^2 <= C M r^4`; it does **not** give
> `int_W F^2 <= C M Vol(W)`.  Critical Sobolev absorption still survives
> through `A_W^2 ||F||_{L^2(W)} <= C r^2 sqrt(M)`, but the unweighted
> moment bounds and the time-uniform `H_3` input must be derived from a
> current per-component first-exit energy, not from a Whitney-volume-normal
> bound.  See `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md`, which
> supersedes Sections 5--13 of this note wherever they use (5.2) or treat
> current `gamma(t)` as already controlled.

> **CORRECTION (TTCS Step 21).** Sections 6 and 8 of the original version
> contained a scaling error: curvature has dimension length⁻², so under
> metric rescaling `g̃ = ℓ⁻²g` the rescaled curvature is `|Rm(g̃)| = ℓ²|Rm(g)|`,
> and `F` is NOT invariant.  The raw Stampacchia output on the rescaled ball
> is `ℓ²F ≤ C`, not `F ≤ C`.  The correct pointwise output is from A03's
> `q → 3q/2` weighted-moment iteration (Section 8 below, replacing the
> original Stampacchia step): `|aRm| ≤ Cγ/t`, giving `|aRm| = O(1)` at
> the smoothing time.  The parabolic Sobolev exponent, BG transfer, and
> a₀-cancellation in the critical absorption remain valid.  The volume
> power in (6.2) is corrected to `Vol^{3/2}`.

## 1. Purpose

This note derives the conditional finite-exponent smoothing lemma for the
normalized cutoff flow

\[
  \partial_tg=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}_g+g),\qquad a=\chi^2,\quad 0\le a\le1,
\]

on a four-dimensional closed Riemannian manifold.  It does not prove a
Ricci-pinching gap and does not settle Yau Problem 26.  All statements below
hold on a provisional first-exit interval on which the evolving metric satisfies
the hypotheses stated in the lemma.

The key advance over Steps 19–20 is an actual PDE output: under the stated
provisional conditions, the four-step chain

\[
  q{=}2\text{ energy}\;\longrightarrow\;
  \text{4D parabolic Sobolev}\;\longrightarrow\;
  q{=}3\text{ + time cutoff}\;\longrightarrow\;
  \text{local boundedness}
\]

produces a uniform curvature bound on each Whitney ball at positive time,
independent of the cutoff level `chi_0` and of collapsed volume.  Critical
absorption is used at the two fixed exponents `q=2` and `q=3` only; the final
step uses the established time-uniform spatial `L^3` as a supercritical
potential (`3 > n/2 = 2` for `n = 4`).

## 2. Hypotheses (provisional first-exit)

Let `B_{5r}(p)` be one support component.  Assume:

**(H1)** Per-component maximal-function control at scale `6r`:
\[
  \mathcal M_{6r}(|\operatorname{Rm}_0|^2)(p)\le K_0.
\]

**(H2)** Metric comparability on `B_{5r}(p)\times[0,T]`, `T=\theta r^2`:
\[
  \Lambda^{-1}g_0\le g(t)\le\Lambda g_0.
\]

**(H3)** Relative Sobolev persistence on `B_{5r}(p)` with constant `A^2`.

**(H4)** Small critical product:
\[
  \gamma:=A^2\|F_0\|_{L^2(B_{5r}(p))}\le\varepsilon_0,
\]
where `F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}` and
`\varepsilon_0=\varepsilon_0(c,L,\Lambda)` is a numerical constant depending
only on the cutoff parameter `c`, the Lipschitz constant `L` of `\chi`, and
the comparability `\Lambda`.

## 3. Bishop–Gromov energy transfer to Whitney balls

Fix `y\in B_{4r}(p)` with `\chi_0=\chi(y)>0`.  Set `\ell=cr\chi_0`,
`a_0=\chi_0^2`, `W=B_\ell(y)`.

Since `B_\ell(y)\subset B_{5r}(p)` (ensured by `c<1` and `d(y,p)<4r`), the
integral comparison gives

\[
  \int_W|\operatorname{Rm}_0|^2\,d\mu_0
  \le\int_{B_{5r}}|\operatorname{Rm}_0|^2\,d\mu_0
  \le K_0\operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{5r}).
\]

Bishop–Gromov on `(M^4,g_0)` with `\operatorname{Ric}\ge-3g_0` gives

\[
  \operatorname{Vol}_0(B_\ell(y))
  \ge c_{\mathrm{BG}}\left(\frac\ell{5r}\right)^4
     \operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{5r}(p))
  =c_{\mathrm{BG}}\left(\frac{c\chi_0}{5}\right)^4
     \operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{5r}).
\]

Therefore

\[
  \ell^4\fint_W|\operatorname{Rm}_0|^2
  \le(cr\chi_0)^4\cdot
    \frac{K_0\operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{5r})}
         {c_{\mathrm{BG}}(c\chi_0/5)^4\operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{5r})}
  =\frac{5^4}{c_{\mathrm{BG}}}\,K_0\,r^4.
\]

The `\chi_0` cancels exactly.  Hence

\[
\boxed{
  \ell^4\fint_W F_0^2\,d\mu_0
  \le C(c)\,K_0\,r^4,
  \qquad
  \gamma_W:=A_W^2\|F_0\|_{L^2(W)}
  \le C\,r^2\sqrt{1+K_0}.
}
\tag{3.1}
\]

By (H2)–(H3), the same bound holds at time `t` with constant
`C(\Lambda)\gamma_W`.

## 4. Whitney-ball setup

On `W=B_\ell(y)`:

\[
  (1-Lc)^2a_0\le a\le(1+Lc)^2a_0,
  \qquad
  \frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}=4|\nabla\chi|^2\le\frac{4L^2}{r^2}.
\]

Nested balls: `W=B_\ell(y)\supset W_1=B_{3\ell/4}\supset W_2=B_{\ell/2}
\supset W_3=B_{\ell/4}\supset W_4=B_{\ell/8}\supset W_5=B_{\ell/16}`.

Whitney rescaling: `\tilde x=(x{-}y)/\ell`, `\tilde t=a_0t/\ell^2`.  On the
rescaled unit ball `\tilde B_1`:

- Operator `\partial_{\tilde t}-\tilde a\,\tilde\Delta` with
  `\tilde a=a/a_0\in[\lambda,\Lambda_W]`, uniformly parabolic.
- Rescaled time: `\tilde T=a_0T/\ell^2=\theta/c^2`, independent of `\chi_0`.
- Rescaled Ricci: `\ell^2\operatorname{Ric}=O(c^2r^2)`, negligibly small.
- Rescaled Sobolev and BG constants: uniformly bounded, dimension-dependent.

Under the metric rescaling `g̃ = ℓ⁻²g`, the curvature transforms as
`|Rm(g̃)|_{g̃} = ℓ² |Rm(g)|_g`.  The natural rescaled regularization is
`F̃ = (1 + |Rm(g̃)|²)^{1/2} ≈ ℓ²F` when `ℓ²|Rm| ≫ 1`.  For the
near-Einstein initial data with `|Rm| ~ O(1)`, the rescaled curvature
`ℓ²|Rm| ~ c²r²χ₀² ≪ 1` is SMALL on the rescaled ball.
The energy estimates below work with the ORIGINAL `F` and the
degenerate operator `∂_t - aΔ` made uniformly parabolic by the Whitney
reduction.  The pointwise bound is obtained by A03's `q → 3q/2` Moser
iteration on the weighted moments `H_q = ∫η² a^{q-2} F^q`, which
avoids metric rescaling entirely.

## 5. Step A — `q=2` energy estimate

Use the power inequality from Step 20, Section 3, at `q=2` with spatial cutoff
`\eta` supported on `W_1` and `|\nabla\eta|\le C/\ell`.  After integrating the
`\nabla^2a` terms by parts (using `|E|\le CF` and `|\nabla E|\le C|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|`):

\[
\begin{aligned}
  \frac d{dt}\int\eta^2F^2\,d\mu+c_2\int\eta^2a|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,d\mu
  &\le C_2\int\eta^2aF^3\,d\mu \\
  &\quad+C_2\int\left(\frac{|\nabla a|^2}{a}+a+a|\nabla\eta|^2\right)F^2\,d\mu.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.1}
\]

The reaction is absorbed by Hölder/Sobolev:

\[
  \int\eta^2aF^3=\int aF\cdot(\eta F)^2
  \le C\,a_0\,\|\eta F\|_4^2\,\|F\|_2
  \le C\,\gamma_W
    \left(\int a|\nabla(\eta F)|^2+\ell^{-2}\int a(\eta F)^2\right).
\]

Since `\gamma_W\le Cr^2\sqrt{1+K_0}\le\varepsilon_0`, the gradient part is
absorbed into the LHS dissipation (the factor `a_0` cancels on both sides).

After absorbing and integrating over `[0,T]`:

\[
\boxed{
  \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\int_{W_2}F^2\,d\mu
  +\int_0^T\!\!\int_{W_2}a|\nabla\operatorname{Rm}|^2\,d\mu\,dt
  \le C_A\,(1+K_0)\operatorname{Vol}_0(W),
}
\tag{5.2}
\]

with `C_A` independent of `\chi_0` and collapsed volume.

## 6. Step B — parabolic Sobolev embedding

In four spatial dimensions, the standard parabolic interpolation inequality
(Ladyzhenskaya/Gagliardo–Nirenberg) gives, for `u\in L^\infty([0,T];L^2)\cap
L^2([0,T];H^1)` on a Riemannian ball of uniform geometry:

\[
  \int_0^T\!\!\int|u|^3\,d\mu\,dt
  \le C_{\mathrm{PS}}
    \left(\sup_t\int u^2\right)^{1/2}
    \int_0^T\!\!\int|\nabla u|^2\,d\mu\,dt.
\tag{6.1}
\]

The exponent `3=2(n{+}2)/n` is specific to `n=4`.

In the rescaled Whitney picture, the diffusivity is `a\approx a_0` and the
effective gradient dissipation is `a_0\int|\nabla F|^2`.  Applying (6.1) to the
Step A outputs on the inner ball `W_3`:

\[
\boxed{
  \int_0^T\!\!\int_{W_3}F^3\,d\mu\,dt
  \le C_B\,(1+K_0)^{3/2}\frac{\operatorname{Vol}_0(W)^{3/2}}{a_0^{1/2}}.
}
\tag{6.2}
\]

A03's weighted formulation uses `H_2 = ∫η²F²` (no `a`-weight at `q=2`)
and `H_3 = ∫η²aF³` (weight `a` at `q=3`).  The spacetime integral of
`H_3` is bounded by the absorption:

\[
  \int_0^TH_3(s)\,ds\le C\gamma\,H_2(0).
\tag{6.3}
\]

This is Equation (2.2) of A03's Step 20 note.  All factors are
independent of `χ_0` and collapsed volume because `γ` and `H_2(0)`
have the BG cancellation from Section 3.

## 7. Step C — `q=3` with time cutoff

On the rescaled cylinder `\tilde B_{1/4}\times[0,\tilde T]`, introduce:

- Time cutoff: `\varphi(\tilde t)=0` for `\tilde t<\tilde\delta`,
  `\varphi=1` for `\tilde t\ge2\tilde\delta`,
  `|\varphi'|\le C/\tilde\delta`.
- Spatial cutoff: `\tilde\eta` on `\tilde B_{1/8}\subset\tilde B_{1/4}`.

The `q=3` power inequality with these cutoffs:

\[
\begin{aligned}
  \frac d{d\tilde t}\int\varphi^2\tilde\eta^2F^3\,d\tilde\mu
  +c_3\int\varphi^2\tilde\eta^2F|\tilde\nabla F|^2\,d\tilde\mu
  &\le C_3\int\varphi^2\tilde\eta^2F^4\,d\tilde\mu \\
  &\quad+2\varphi\varphi'\int\tilde\eta^2F^3\,d\tilde\mu
        +\text{(cutoff spatial terms)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.1}
\]

The reaction `\int\varphi^2\tilde\eta^2F^4` is absorbed by the same
Hölder/Sobolev mechanism at `q=3`:

\[
  \int(\varphi\tilde\eta F^{3/2})^2\cdot F
  \le\gamma_W\bigl(\|\nabla(\varphi\tilde\eta F^{3/2})\|_2^2+\cdots\bigr),
\]

absorbing the gradient part against the LHS dissipation (factor `9/4`
from `\nabla(F^{3/2})=(3/2)F^{1/2}\nabla F`).  The coefficient for `q=3`
is `9\gamma_W/4$`, still small.  Since `\varphi(0)=0`, the initial term
vanishes, and the time-derivative source is bounded by Step B:

\[
  \int_0^{\tilde T}|\varphi'|\int\tilde\eta^2F^3\,d\tilde\mu\,d\tilde t
  \le\frac C{\tilde\delta}\int_0^{\tilde T}\!\!\int_{\tilde B_{1/4}}F^3
  \le\frac{\tilde C_B}{\tilde\delta}.
\]

After absorption, since `\varphi=1` on `[\,2\tilde\delta,\tilde T\,]`:

\[
\boxed{
  \sup_{\tilde t\in[2\tilde\delta,\,\tilde T]}
  \int_{\tilde B_{1/8}}F^3\,d\tilde\mu
  \le\frac{C_C}{\tilde\delta},
}
\tag{7.2}
\]

with `C_C` depending only on the rescaled Sobolev constant and the bound
`\tilde C_B`.  All independent of `\chi_0` and collapsed volume.

Converting to original variables (`\tilde\delta=a_0\delta/\ell^2=\delta/(c^2r^2)`):

\[
  \sup_{t\in[2\delta,\,T]}\int_{B_{\ell/8}(y)}F^3\,d\mu
  \le\frac{C\,c^2r^2}{\delta}\,\ell^4.
\]

The L³ average `\fint_{B_{\ell/8}}F^3` is bounded by a constant depending
only on `\delta/(c^2r^2)`, the Sobolev data, and `K_0`.

## 8. Step D — weighted Moser iteration `q → 3q/2` (from A03)

> The original version used Stampacchia on the rescaled ball, but this
> requires the rescaled curvature `\tilde F = (1+\ell^4|Rm|^2)^{1/2}`,
> not the original `F`.  The raw Stampacchia output is `\ell^2F \le C`,
> i.e., `|aRm| \le Cr^{-2}`, which is weaker than needed.
> The correct mechanism is A03's weighted-moment iteration,
> which works entirely in the original metric.

From Steps A–C, the weighted cubic potential satisfies (A03 equation 2.3):

\[
  A^4H_3(t)\le\frac{C\gamma^3}{t},
  \qquad t\in(0,T].
\tag{8.1}
\]

This makes the curvature reaction in the `q`-th power inequality a time-dependent
potential of strength `C(r^{-2}+\gamma^3/t)` on `[t/2,t]`.  The recurrence
`q_{j+1}=3q_j/2` with base `q_0=2`, applied on nested cylinders
`Q_{j+1}\Subset Q_j\subset B_{\ell/2}\times[t/2,t]`, gives (A03 equation 11.3):

\[
  M_{q_{j+1}}(Q_{j+1})^{1/q_{j+1}}
  \le (CA^2)^{2/(3q_j)}
  \left[Cq_j^\sigma4^j(t^{-1}+r^{-2})\right]^{1/q_j}
  M_{q_j}(Q_j)^{1/q_j}.
\tag{8.2}
\]

The exponent sums `\sum1/q_j=3/q_0=3/2` and
`\sum(j+\log q_j)/q_j<\infty` guarantee convergence of the product.
The endpoint is:

\[
\boxed{
  \|aF(t)\|_\infty\le C\gamma/t
  \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
  |a\operatorname{Rm}(t)|\le C\gamma/t.
}
\tag{8.3}
\]

At the smoothing time `t=\theta r^2`:

\[
  |a\operatorname{Rm}|\le\frac{C\gamma}{\theta r^2}
  =\frac{C\sqrt{1+K_0}}{\theta}=O(1).
\]

For the defect, the same iteration starting from `q_0=6` and `J_6(0)\le\delta^6V`
gives (A03 equation 11.4):

\[
\boxed{
  |aE(t)|\le C\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3}.
}
\tag{8.4}
\]

All constants are independent of `\chi_0` and collapsed volume because the
weighted moments `H_q`, `J_m`, the BG energy transfer, and the Sobolev product
all have the cancellation from Section 3.

**What (8.3)–(8.4) give on the transition and plateau.**

- Plateau (`\chi_0=1`): `a=1`, so `|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C\gamma/t=O(1)`.
  The curvature is bounded.
- Transition (`\chi_0\to0`): `a=\chi_0^2`, so
  `|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C\gamma/(t\chi_0^2)` may be large.  The velocity
  estimate controls only bilipschitz metric displacement,
  `\int_0^T|aE|\,dt\le C\delta\,T\cdot(r^2/T)^{1/3}=O(\delta r^2)`,
  independent of `\chi_0`; it does not control curvature closeness because
  curvature contains second spatial derivatives.  No pointwise transition
  curvature bound should be inferred here.

The weighted bound `|aRm|=O(1)` is the correct output for the continuation
argument.  It does NOT give `|Rm|\le C` with constant independent of `\chi_0`,
but it does give uniform control on the metric speed `|aE|` and on all weighted
curvature expressions entering the energy and defect inequalities.

**Conditional status.**  The iteration (8.2) requires the weak nested
time-space estimate (A03 equation 11.1) on every nested cylinder,
uniformly with finite-neighbor outer terms.  This is the remaining
mathematical task for the zero-order curvature layer.

## 9. Conditional Finite-Exponent Smoothing Lemma

**Lemma.** Under hypotheses (H1)–(H4) with `T=\theta r^2`, `\theta<c^2/4`:
for every `y\in B_{4r}(p)` with `\chi(y)=\chi_0>0`, setting `\ell=cr\chi_0`,
and for every `\delta>0`:

1. *Time-uniform L²*:
   `\sup_{t}\int_{B_{\ell/2}}F^2\le C(1+K_0)\operatorname{Vol}(W)`.

2. *Spacetime L³*:
   `\int_0^T\int_{B_{\ell/4}}F^3\,d\mu\,dt` is bounded.

3. *Time-uniform spatial L³*:
   `\sup_{t\ge2\delta}\int_{B_{\ell/8}}F^3` is bounded.

4. *Weighted pointwise bound* (from A03 `q\to3q/2` Moser iteration):
   `|a\operatorname{Rm}(t)|\le C\gamma/t`, hence `|a\operatorname{Rm}|=O(1)`
   at `t=\theta r^2`.  Also `|aE(t)|\le C\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}`.

All bounds are independent of `\chi_0` and collapsed volume.

**Proof.** Steps A–C above provide time-uniform weighted cubic potential
`H_3(t)\le C\gamma H_2(0)/t`.  Step D uses A03's `q\to3q/2` Moser
iteration on nested cylinders with convergent exponent products to produce
the pointwise weighted bounds (8.3)–(8.4).

## 10. Consequences for the continuation argument

The lemma gives weighted curvature and defect control on every Whitney ball.

**Metric drift.** `\int_0^T|aE|\,dt\le C\delta\,T^{2/3}\,r^{2/3}
=O(\delta r^2)$, independent of `\chi_0`.  Metric comparability (H2) is
maintained for sufficiently small `\delta` and `r`.

**Weighted curvature.** `|a\operatorname{Rm}|=O(1)` at the smoothing time.
This does NOT give `|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C$ with constant independent of
`\chi_0$; in the transition, `|\operatorname{Rm}|$ may be `O(1/\chi_0^2)`.
The metric displacement estimate gives bilipschitz comparison there, but not
curvature closeness to the initial metric.  The corrected Step 22 formulation
does not use pointwise transition curvature control.

**Defect energy.** From the triangular `Q$ estimate (Step 20, Section 7):
`Q_{\mathrm{support}}(T)\le e^{CT/r^2}Q_{\mathrm{support}}(0)`.  The weighted
curvature bound provides the potential `a|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C\gamma/t$ for
the local defect inequality.  With `\gamma/t=O(1/r^2)$ at `t=\theta r^2$, the
finite-neighbor coupling has bounded coefficients.

**Controlled charts.** On the plateau (`\chi_0=1`), `|a\operatorname{Rm}|=O(1)`
gives `|\operatorname{Rm}|=O(1)$, so the harmonic-coordinate equation produces a
controlled chart.  Through Step 8 tensor-deficit densities and Derdziński's
Proposition 5, the forbidden calibrated Einstein germ is obtained.  In the
transition, no chart is needed because the metric is essentially unchanged.

## 11. Relation to A03 weighted-moment hierarchy

A03's formulation uses the weighted moments `H_q=\int\eta^2a^{q-2}F^q` with
Sobolev variable `v_q=\eta a^{(q-1)/2}F^{q/2}`.  Their result (2.3):

\[
  A^4H_3(t)\le\frac{C\gamma^3}{t}
\]

is the time-decay version of Step C.  The backwards averaging that produces
this `1/t$ decay is equivalent to the time-cutoff mechanism: from
`\int_0^tH_3\le C\gamma H_2(0)` and `H_3'\le Cr^{-2}H_3$`, a good
intermediate time exists with `H_3(t_1)\le C\gamma H_2(0)/t_1$`, and forward
propagation from `t_1$ gives the uniform bound.

The two approaches are complementary: the direct weighted moments are cleaner
for the zero-order curvature hierarchy, while the Whitney rescaling makes the
operator uniformly parabolic for the subsequent derivative/Bernstein estimates.

## 12. Per-component versus total-support energy

A03 (message #292) correctly noted that total-support energy does not
automatically imply per-Whitney-ball smallness.  The resolution is in
Section 3: the maximal-function selection in (H1) gives per-component control
`\fint_{B_{5r}(p)}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le K_0$, and Bishop–Gromov comparison
from the component center to any interior Whitney ball cancels the `\chi_0^4$
factor in `\ell^4$ against the `(c\chi_0/5)^4$ volume ratio.

The centered per-component budget IS sufficient.  No additional per-Whitney-ball
hypothesis is needed beyond (H1).

## 13. What remains for the first-exit closure

The finite-exponent lemma and the `q\to3q/2` iteration are conditional on
(H1)–(H4) and on the weak nested time-space estimate (A03 eq. 11.1).

**Self-improving structure.** Per A03 message #294, the zero-order first-exit
does NOT require quantitative pointwise control of `\chi\nabla(aE)` or of
the connection.  All Hessian-`a` terms integrate by parts; fixed cutoff
gradients, relative Sobolev constants, and volume comparison transfer under
bilipschitz metric comparability.  The provisional first-exit quantities are:

1. **Metric comparability (H2)**: improved by the integrable defect velocity
   `|aE|\le C\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}`.

2. **Sobolev persistence (H3)**: follows from metric comparability on fixed
   domains.  Self-improving.

3. **Current-time critical energy**: must be maintained small by a first-exit
   argument.  The `q=2` energy inequality gives `\sup_t\int F^2\le C(1+K_0)Vol`,
   so `\gamma(t)=A^2\|F(t)\|_2\le C\gamma(0)`.  This needs explicit
   writing but uses the same absorption mechanism.

4. **Triangular defect `Q/A\to0`**: from the multiplicative coupling
   `Q'_\alpha\le Cr^{-2}\sum Q_\beta`.

5. **Weak nested time-space estimate** (A03 eq. 11.1): the load-bearing
   remaining derivation.  All algebraic and exponent structure has been
   verified; the task is to prove it uniformly with the finite-neighbor
   outer terms from the exact evolving tensor equations.

6. **Adaptation of Wang's smooth-extension theorem**: terminal `|aRm|\le C\gamma/t`
   is expected to generate derivative bounds internally, but this adaptation
   from `-2aRic` to `-2a(Ric+g)` must be written.

## 14. Broader research position

This lemma addresses only the critical four-dimensional negative
LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun laboratory.  Even if the full first-exit closure is
established, it would prove only the negative-branch Ricci-pinching theorem
for this specific family.  The positive branch, higher dimensions `n\ge5`,
the full interval statement, and the Lean 4 formalization remain open.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Step 22 correction: this Step 21 script is retained only as arithmetic history.
# Its final local-boundedness and transition-curvature lines use a stronger
# Whitney-volume-normal energy interpretation than the available component
# budget provides.  Use step22_energy_normalization.py and
# step22_first_exit_energy.py for the corrected current-energy bookkeeping.
"""
Step 21: Conditional finite-exponent smoothing verification.

Verify the three-step route:
  q=2 energy  →  parabolic Sobolev (4D)  →  q=3 + time cutoff
that produces time-uniform spatial L³ on each Whitney ball,
then local boundedness from the supercritical potential.

All constants are tracked for independence from chi_0 and collapsed volume.
"""
import numpy as np

n = 4  # spatial dimension
print("=" * 72)
print("FINITE-EXPONENT SMOOTHING: KEY ARITHMETIC VERIFICATION")
print("=" * 72)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Parabolic Sobolev exponent
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
p_star = 2 * (n + 2) / n
print(f"\n1. PARABOLIC SOBOLEV EXPONENT (n={n})")
print(f"   p* = 2(n+2)/n = {p_star:.1f}")
print(f"   This is L^3 spacetime from L^inf_t L^2_x ∩ L^2_t H^1_x")
assert p_star == 3.0, f"Expected 3, got {p_star}"
print("   PASS")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Supercritical condition for local boundedness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
critical_exp = n / 2  # n/2 = 2 for n=4
print(f"\n2. SUPERCRITICAL CONDITION FOR LOCAL BOUNDEDNESS")
print(f"   n/2 = {critical_exp}")
print(f"   L^3_spatial is supercritical: 3 > {critical_exp}  ✓")
print(f"   Standard Stampacchia/Moser local L^∞ applies with L^3 potential")
assert 3 > critical_exp
print("   PASS")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. BG energy transfer to Whitney balls
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n3. BISHOP-GROMOV ENERGY TRANSFER")
c_param = 0.1   # Whitney parameter
L_param = 2.0   # |grad chi| <= L/r
K0 = 15100.0    # Noether mean curvature bound (65/6 * 8pi^2)
r_star = 0.003  # Li scale

# For a support B_{5r}(p) with maximal-function control:
# fint_{B_{5r}} |Rm|^2 <= K0
#
# For a Whitney ball B_ell(y) with ell = c*r*chi0, inside B_{4r}(p):
# BG comparison: Vol(B_ell(y)) / Vol(B_{5r}(p)) >= c_BG * (ell/(5r))^n
# Hence: fint_{B_ell} |Rm|^2 <= K0 * Vol(B_{5r}) / Vol(B_ell)
#                                <= K0 * (5r/ell)^n / c_BG
# And: ell^n * fint_{B_ell} |Rm|^2 <= K0 * (5r)^n / c_BG
#                                    = C * K0 * r^n
# chi_0 cancels completely!

for chi0 in [1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 1e-4, 1e-6]:
    ell = c_param * r_star * chi0
    # ell^4 * K0 * (5r/ell)^4 = K0 * (5r)^4 independent of chi0
    Li_dim = K0 * (5 * r_star)**4  # = K0 * 625 * r^4
    print(f"   chi0={chi0:.0e}: ell={ell:.2e}, "
          f"ell^4 fint |Rm|^2 <= {Li_dim:.4e} (independent of chi0)")

gamma = c_param**2 * r_star**2 * np.sqrt(1 + K0)
print(f"\n   Critical product gamma = c^2 r^2 sqrt(1+K0) = {gamma:.6e}")
print(f"   This is small: {gamma < 0.01}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Absorption thresholds at q=2 and q=3
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n4. ABSORPTION THRESHOLDS AT q=2 AND q=3")
# At exponent q, the chain-rule coefficient is q^2/4.
# Absorption needs: gamma * q^2 / 4 <= epsilon_0 (say 0.1)
eps_0 = 0.1
for q in [2, 3, 4, 6, 10]:
    coeff = q**2 / 4
    threshold = gamma * coeff
    ok = threshold < eps_0
    print(f"   q={q:2d}: coefficient q^2/4 = {coeff:6.1f}, "
          f"gamma * coeff = {threshold:.6e}, "
          f"{'OK' if ok else 'FAIL'} (need < {eps_0})")

max_q_feasible = int(np.sqrt(4 * eps_0 / gamma))
print(f"   Max feasible q with current gamma: ~{max_q_feasible}")
print(f"   Only q=2 and q=3 are needed; rest comes from L^3 potential theory")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Whitney time independence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n5. WHITNEY TIME SCALING")
theta = c_param**2 / 8  # physical flow time parameter
print(f"   Physical flow time: T = theta*r^2 = {theta * r_star**2:.2e}")
for chi0 in [1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 1e-4, 1e-6]:
    ell = c_param * r_star * chi0
    a0 = chi0**2
    rescaled_time = a0 * theta * r_star**2 / ell**2
    print(f"   chi0={chi0:.0e}: rescaled time a0*T/ell^2 = {rescaled_time:.4f} "
          f"= theta/c^2 = {theta/c_param**2:.4f}")

print(f"   All equal: rescaled time = theta/c^2 = {theta/c_param**2:.4f}")
print("   PASS: independent of chi_0")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Parabolic interpolation check
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n6. PARABOLIC INTERPOLATION")
print(f"   Standard inequality (n={n}):")
print(f"   int_0^T int |u|^{{2(n+2)/n}} <= C (sup_t int u^2)^{{2/n}} * int_0^T int |grad u|^2")
print(f"   Exponent: 2(n+2)/n = {2*(n+2)/n:.0f}")
print(f"   Powers: (sup L^2)^(2/n) = (sup L^2)^(1/2) for n=4")
print(f"   This converts L^inf_t L^2 ∩ L^2_t H^1 → L^3 spacetime")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Time cutoff source control
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n7. TIME-CUTOFF SOURCE CONTROL FOR q=3")
print(f"   Time cutoff phi(t): phi=0 for t<delta, phi=1 for t>2*delta")
print(f"   Source: int phi' * eta^2 * F^3 dt <= (C/delta) * int_0^T int F^3 dt")
print(f"   The spacetime L^3 integral from Step 2 is bounded")
print(f"   So the time-cutoff source is O(1/delta), finite for any delta > 0")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Summary chain
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n8. COMPLETE CHAIN ON ONE WHITNEY BALL (rescaled to unit)")
print(f"   Step A: q=2 energy (critical absorption, gamma small)")
print(f"     → sup_t int_{{B_{{1/2}}}} F^2 + int_0^{{T~}} int |grad F|^2 <= C1")
print(f"   Step B: parabolic Sobolev (4D, free)")
print(f"     → int_0^{{T~}} int_{{B_{{1/4}}}} F^3 <= C2")
print(f"   Step C: q=3 + time cutoff (critical absorption, same gamma)")
print(f"     → sup_{{t~>=2delta~}} int_{{B_{{1/8}}}} F^3 <= C3(delta)")
print(f"   Step D: Stampacchia local boundedness (L^3 potential, 3 > n/2 = 2)")
print(f"     → sup_{{B_{{1/16}} x [3delta~, T~]}} F <= C4(delta)")
print(f"")
print(f"   All constants C1-C4 are independent of chi_0 and collapsed volume.")
print(f"   Critical absorption is needed at q=2 and q=3 only.")
print(f"   Threshold: gamma = {gamma:.6e} < epsilon_0 = {eps_0}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. Consequence for weighted curvature and metric drift
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
print(f"\n9. CONSEQUENCES")
print(f"   On plateau (chi0=1):   |Rm| <= C4, |E| <= delta")
print(f"   On transition (chi0→0): a*|Rm| = chi0^2*|Rm| <= chi0^2*C4 → 0")
print(f"   Metric drift: int_0^T |aE| dt <= a*C4*T = chi0^2*C4*theta*r^2 → 0")
print(f"   Metric comparability is maintained for small r")

print(f"\n{'='*72}")
print(f"ALL CHECKS PASS")
print(f"{'='*72}")

# Step 22 superseding note

The Step 21 route assessment is superseded by `workspace/plans/route_assessment_step22.md` and `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md`.  The Step 21 text treats the time-uniform `H_3` input as if it follows from a Whitney-volume-normal `L^2` estimate; the available component budget gives only the scale-invariant mean and critical Sobolev product.  Current energy persistence must be proved as a finite-neighbor first-exit estimate.  Also remove the transition inference that small metric displacement keeps curvature close to its initial value.

# Route assessment after Step 21

## What changed

Step 21 developed the conditional finite-exponent smoothing lemma: the
two-step (q=2, q=3) energy argument produces a time-controlled weighted
cubic potential H_3(t) ≤ Cγ H_2(0)/t, after which A03's q→3q/2 Moser
iteration gives the pointwise weighted bounds |aRm| ≤ Cγ/t and
|aE| ≤ Cδ(r²/t)^{1/3}.

TTCS found a critical scaling correction: curvature has dimension length⁻²,
so the metric-rescaling approach to local boundedness gives ℓ²F ≤ C (i.e.,
|aRm| ≤ Cr⁻²), not F ≤ C with constant independent of χ₀.  The correct
mechanism avoiding this overestimate is A03's weighted-moment Moser iteration,
which works entirely in the original metric.

A03 (messages #294–295) further clarified that quantitative pointwise
derivative control is NOT needed for the zero-order first-exit closure.
All Hessian-a terms integrate by parts; cutoff gradients transfer under
bilipschitz comparability.  The derivative/Bernstein estimate is no longer
load-bearing for the zero-order argument.

## Established

1. BG energy transfer: ℓ⁴ fint |Rm|² ≤ CK₀r⁴ (χ₀ cancels exactly).
2. Critical a₀-cancellation in the Sobolev absorption at q=2 and q=3.
3. Parabolic Sobolev exponent 2(n+2)/n = 3 for n=4.
4. Time-cutoff mechanism: spacetime L³ controls the q=3 time-derivative source.
5. A03 q→3q/2 infinite product converges; endpoint gives |aF| ≤ Cγ/t.
6. No derivative estimate needed for zero-order first-exit.

## Corrected (from TTCS)

- Curvature rescaling: under g̃ = ℓ⁻²g, |Rm(g̃)| = ℓ²|Rm(g)|.
  F is NOT invariant under metric rescaling.
- Volume power in parabolic Sobolev: Vol^{3/2}, not Vol².
- Current-time γ(t) must be maintained by the first-exit system, not
  assumed from γ(0) alone.
- Bootstrap closure (Section 13) requires the first-exit structure
  explicitly, not just a verbal assertion.

## Current mathematical state

The analytic bridge now has a clean structure:

1. Fixed q=2,3 energy → cubic potential H₃ (Steps A–C, valid)
2. q→3q/2 Moser iteration → pointwise |aRm| ≤ Cγ/t (A03 Sections 10–11)
3. Triangular defect → Q/A → 0 (Step 20 Section 7)
4. Metric comparability from integrable |aE| (A03 Section 9)

The remaining derivation is the weak nested time-space estimate (A03 eq. 11.1)
uniformly with finite-neighbor outer terms.  Once this is proved, the first-exit
system closes without derivative estimates and without metric rescaling.

## What this does NOT settle

- Only the critical four-dimensional negative LeBrun/Ishida-LeBrun laboratory
- Positive branch, higher dimensions n≥5, and Lean formalization remain open
- The full interval statement of Yau Problem 26 is not resolved

# Step 22: 原研究交接

## 已开展的研究

I began from the Strategist correction to Step 21 and inspected `workspace/notes/step21_finite_exponent_smoothing_lemma.md`, `workspace/plans/route_assessment_step21.md`, A03's weighted Wang hierarchy note, and recent peer messages. I wrote `workspace/scripts/step22_energy_normalization.py`, which demonstrates the corrected Whitney energy bookkeeping: with a nonconcentric 9r buffer, the worst local mean grows like chi0^{-4}, while ell^4 average_W F^2 and A_W^2||F||_2 stay constant. Its final run used M=11, r=0.01, c=0.1 and returned normalized mean factor 6561 and gamma 0.0268646608 independent of chi0 from 1 to 1e-6. I wrote `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md` and `workspace/plans/route_assessment_step22.md` to supersede Step 21's false Whitney-volume-normal energy use. I patched `step21_finite_exponent_smoothing_lemma.md` and `route_assessment_step21.md` with superseding notices and removed the old transition curvature closeness inference. I then wrote `workspace/scripts/step22_first_exit_energy.py`, modeling the corrected graph variable S_alpha=A_alpha^4 H_{2,alpha}; its final run with r=0.003, theta=0.001, N=8, C=12, C_A=1.3 gave Gamma0=1.105975e-03, S amplification 1.315459, Gamma(T)=1.268481e-03 below 4 Gamma0, and verified the graph-semigroup scale A^4 H_3 ~ Gamma^3/t. I wrote an initial weak moment note and script, asked TTCS to verify it, and received crucial corrections. TTCS confirmed the main energy repair but found the nonconcentric volume comparison should use a 9r-type buffer, graph propagation should be in S_alpha with neighbor Sobolev ratios, neighbor dissipations need summed absorption, the cubic potential should use graph semigroup propagation, the weak moment note suppressed cutoff powers, and the time intervals were ordered incorrectly. After reading A02 message #298 and its note on collapse Sobolev behavior, I overwrote `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md` and `workspace/notes/step22_weak_nested_moment_estimate.md` with the repaired versions. I rewrote `workspace/scripts/step22_weak_moment_ledger.py` to track eta,a,F monomials and cutoff powers; it initially failed because I had assigned the outer xi cutoff an eta power in the pointwise product, then after correction it passed, verifying that the reaction uses outer H_3^{1/3} times K_q, K_q <= H_q^{1/2}||v_q||_4^2, same-cutoff H_{2q}^{1/2}=||v_q||_4^2 is false, Whitney spatial cutoff gives 4^k/(c^2 r^2), and the corrected time intervals shrink. I also wrote `workspace/scripts/step22_defect_Q_j6_ledger.py`, which passed and records two stability facts: fixed J_m moments can absorb int F z_m^2 directly with gamma(D+J/r^2), avoiding an H_3~1/t coefficient from zero, and the unweighted Q potential int eta^2 a F |E|^2 is F w^2 for w=eta a^{1/2}E, so the algebra still contains E factors rather than a curvature-only source. All Step 22 scripts ran successfully; the final file check confirmed the updated notes, plan, and four scripts exist, and text scans found only intentional statements rejecting curvature closeness rather than inheriting it. I sent group message #299 summarizing the corrections and file paths.

## 当时的后续问题

Continue the analytic construction from the corrected Step 22 files, not from the superseded Step 21 finite-exponent conclusion. The immediate mathematical task is to turn the corrected framework into an exact tensor-and-graph proof segment. Start with `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md`, `workspace/notes/step22_weak_nested_moment_estimate.md`, `workspace/scripts/step22_weak_moment_ledger.py`, `workspace/scripts/step22_defect_Q_j6_ledger.py`, A03's `Sessions/S0910A03/workspace/notes/step20_weighted_wang_hierarchy_and_whitney_correction.md`, and TTCS verification `trace/ttcs/results/step22_ttcs01_verifier1_integration.md`. Develop the exact curvature power inequality for the normalized cutoff flow d_t g=-2a(Ric+g): include measure evolution, inverse metric variation, F regularization, the algebraic lower-order normalized terms, da*nabla E and Hess(a)*E terms, and the integration by parts that converts Hess(a) into regular |da|^2/a and cutoff terms while retaining full tensor dissipation. Use nested inner/outer cutoffs throughout. Then prove the graph-level q=2 support-energy persistence for S_alpha=A_alpha^4 H_{2,alpha}, with neighbor Sobolev comparability and summed absorption of neighbor dissipations. From that same graph system, derive the positive-time cubic potential A_alpha^4 H_{3,alpha}(t)<=C Gamma_*^3/t using graph semigroup propagation rather than a fixed neighbor star. In parallel, write the fixed J_6 persistence estimate using the direct gamma absorption, and begin the unweighted Q calculation, keeping the target triangular form Q'_alpha<=Cr^{-2}sum Q_beta with no curvature-only additive source. Preserve the distinction between plateau bounded curvature and transition metric displacement: do not use transition curvature closeness. The broader research remains open; this work only strengthens the critical four-dimensional negative route and must later be connected to the Step 8 Derdzinski calibrated-germ contradiction, while positive pinching, arbitrary four-manifolds, n>=5, the full interval proposition, and Lean formalization remain unresolved.

# Step 22: corrected current-energy formulation for cutoff smoothing

> **Step 23 supersedes Sections 4-5.** Equation (4.3) was not proved by
> the absorption in Section 4 because it lacked covering subordination
> and assumed componentwise absorption was automatic.  Step 23 resolves
> both: the exact tensor inequality has ε=0 (no neighbor dissipation),
> and a maximal r-net provides covering subordination.  See
> `step23_cooperative_persistence_theorem.md`.

This note supersedes the energy-normalization parts of `step21_finite_exponent_smoothing_lemma.md` and also repairs the first version of Step 22 after independent TTCS verification and A02 message #298.  The main point is that the available input is a component-scale current energy together with a relative Sobolev coefficient, not a Whitney-volume-normal energy bound.

We study the normalized cutoff flow

\[
\partial_t g=-2aE,\qquad a=\chi^2,
\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,
\qquad F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}.
\]

Constants may depend on dimension, fixed cutoff profiles, bilipschitz comparison, overlap number, and finite neighbor degree.  They must not depend on the cutoff value `chi_0`, collapsed volume, or the number of components.

## 1. Component energy does not imply Whitney-volume energy

Let

\[
U=B_{5r}(p),\qquad W=B_\ell(y),\qquad y\in B_{4r}(p),
\qquad \ell=cr\chi_0,
\qquad 0<\chi_0\le1.
\]

The component input has the form

\[
\int_U F^2\,d\mu \le M\operatorname{Vol}(U),\qquad M\simeq 1+K_0,
\tag{1.1}
\]

or the corresponding current-time first-exit quantity below.  Since `W subset U`, (1.1) yields only

\[
\int_WF^2\le M\operatorname{Vol}(U).
\tag{1.2}
\]

Energy may concentrate inside `W`, so one cannot replace the right side by `CM Vol(W)`.

The volume comparison must be nonconcentric.  Since `U=B_{5r}(p)` and `y in B_{4r}(p)`,

\[
U\subset B_{9r}(y).
\]

The initial Ricci lower bound gives Bishop--Gromov comparison, hence

\[
\operatorname{Vol}_0(W)
\ge b\left(\frac{\ell}{9r}\right)^4\operatorname{Vol}_0(B_{9r}(y))
\ge b\left(\frac{\ell}{9r}\right)^4\operatorname{Vol}_0(U).
\tag{1.3}
\]

At later times this fixed-domain volume relation is transferred only through bilipschitz comparison; bilipschitz comparison itself does not create a new Ricci lower bound.

Combining (1.2) and (1.3),

\[
\fint_WF^2\le C M\left(\frac r\ell\right)^4,
\qquad
\ell^4\fint_WF^2\le CMr^4.
\tag{1.4}
\]

The local mean can therefore grow like `chi_0^{-4}`.  This invalidates every use of

\[
\int_WF^2\le CM\operatorname{Vol}(W)
\]

unless an additional local mean hypothesis or accessible cover supplies it.

## 2. The surviving four-dimensional cancellation

In four dimensions a relative Sobolev coefficient on a ball or fixed support domain has the scaling

\[
A_W^2\lesssim \ell^2\operatorname{Vol}(W)^{-1/2}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_W^2\|F\|_{L^2(W)}
&\lesssim \ell^2\operatorname{Vol}(W)^{-1/2}
       \bigl(M\operatorname{Vol}(U)\bigr)^{1/2}\\
&\lesssim \ell^2\sqrt M\left(\frac r\ell\right)^2
\lesssim r^2\sqrt M.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.1}
\]

Thus critical Sobolev absorption survives collapse only through the product

\[
\gamma=A^2\|F\|_2.
\]

This is also the point of A02 message #298: a thin product or cusp can have raw downstairs `L^2` curvature tending to zero while the relative Sobolev coefficient grows so that `A^2||F||_2` remains order one.  Any argument using a dimension-only downstairs Sobolev constant in a collapsed domain is therefore false.  The current route must carry either relative Sobolev constants on finite-neighbor downstairs domains or work on genuine buffered covers where the cutoff, flow, and mean estimates are transported correctly.

## 3. Correct first-exit energy variable

Take a finite family of supports `U_alpha` and larger buffered domains `U_alpha^+` carrying outer cutoffs.  Let an inner cutoff `eta_alpha` be supported where an outer cutoff `xi_alpha` is identically one.  Define

\[
H_{2,\alpha}(t)=\int_{U_\alpha^+}\xi_\alpha^2 F^2\,d\mu_t,
\qquad
S_\alpha(t)=A_\alpha^4H_{2,\alpha}(t),
\qquad
\Gamma(t)=\sup_\alpha S_\alpha(t)^{1/2}.
\tag{3.1}
\]

Using `S_alpha` rather than bare `H_2` keeps varying Sobolev coefficients visible.  Neighboring coefficients must be comparable:

\[
C_A^{-1}A_\beta\le A_\alpha\le C_AA_\beta
\qquad (\beta\sim\alpha).
\tag{3.2}
\]

This is a geometric input from fixed-domain bilipschitz comparison and the finite-neighbor construction, not an automatic consequence of raw curvature energy.

The initial maximal-function/support construction is intended to give

\[
\Gamma(0)\le Cr^2\sqrt{1+K_0}.
\tag{3.3}
\]

Choosing `r` so that (3.3) is small is the small-energy input for the analytic loop.

## 4. Support-energy persistence with neighbor absorption

The schematic `q=2` tensor inequality has the form

\[
\frac{d}{dt}H_{2,\alpha}+cD_{2,\alpha}
\le C\left(r^{-2}H_{2,\widehat\alpha}+H_{3,\widehat\alpha}\right),
\tag{4.1}
\]

where `widehat alpha` denotes a bounded neighbor enlargement and

\[
D_{2,\alpha}\simeq \int |\nabla(\eta_\alpha a^{1/2}F)|^2,
\qquad
H_{3,\widehat\alpha}=\int \xi_\alpha^2aF^3.
\]

The reaction is absorbed using the outer component energy:

\[
H_{3,\widehat\alpha}
=\int aF(\xi_\alpha F)^2
\le C\gamma_{\widehat\alpha}(t)
      \left(D_{2,\widehat\alpha}+r^{-2}H_{2,\widehat\alpha}\right).
\tag{4.2}
\]

Here `xi_alpha=1` on the inner testing support, so the unweighted `L^2` factor is truly controlled by the outer `H_2` quantity.  The dissipations on the right generally belong to neighbor domains; they cannot be absorbed one component at a time into `D_{2,alpha}`.  The absorption must be performed before expansion or after summing over a bounded-degree weighted graph.  A clean graph form is

\[
S_\alpha'(t)
\le Cr^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}
\frac{A_\alpha^4}{A_\beta^4}S_\beta(t),
\tag{4.3}
\]

provided `\Gamma(t)<=\Gamma_*` and `C\Gamma_*` is inside the absorption range.  From (3.2),

\[
S_\alpha'(t)
\le C C_A^4 r^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}S_\beta(t).
\tag{4.4}
\]

For a graph of degree at most `N`, the sup norm or graph-semigroup estimate gives, for `T=theta r^2`,

\[
\sup_\alpha S_\alpha(t)
\le e^{C C_A^4N\theta}\sup_\alpha S_\alpha(0),
\qquad 0\le t\le T.
\tag{4.5}
\]

Thus

\[
\Gamma(t)\le e^{C C_A^4N\theta/2}\Gamma(0).
\tag{4.6}
\]

With `r` chosen small enough for (3.3) and `theta` chosen fixed but sufficiently small, the first-exit bound for `Gamma` improves.  This is the support-energy statement needed later; it is not a Whitney-volume-normal bound.

## 5. Cubic potential from the same current energy

The same weighted estimates give a spacetime cubic bound

\[
\int_0^t\sum_\alpha H_{3,\alpha}(s)\,ds
\le C\Gamma_*\sum_\alpha H_{2,\alpha}(0),
\tag{5.1}
\]

with bounded overlap and neighbor enlargement.  For pointwise-in-time control of `H_3`, the fixed `q=3` estimate has the form

\[
\frac{d}{dt}H_{3,\alpha}
\le Cr^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}H_{3,\beta},
\tag{5.2}
\]

again after absorption by `Gamma_*`.  Positive-time spreading is along the graph, not confined to one fixed neighbor star.  The correct expression is therefore graph-semigroup propagation:

\[
H_3(t)\le C t^{-1}
\exp\!\bigl(C(t/r^2)\mathcal A\bigr)
\int_0^t H_3(s)\,ds,
\tag{5.3}
\]

where `A` is the bounded-degree adjacency operator, so row sums are bounded by `e^{CNt/r^2}`.  After multiplying by the comparable `A_alpha^4`,

\[
A_\alpha^4H_{3,\alpha}(t)
\le \frac{C\Gamma_*^3}{t}.
\tag{5.4}
\]

This is the desired cubic potential, but it depends on the current support-energy loop (4.3)--(4.6).

## 6. Terminal curvature and transition region

A03's weighted `q -> 3q/2` product remains a valid conditional implication once the weak nested time-space estimate is proved.  It yields

\[
|aF(t)|\le C\Gamma_*/t,
\qquad
|aE(t)|\le C\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}.
\tag{6.1}
\]

A weaker rescaled boundedness route gives at best

\[
|a\operatorname{Rm}(T)|\le Cr^{-2},
\qquad T=\theta r^2.
\tag{6.2}
\]

This weaker terminal estimate is still enough for finite curvature on plateau buffers where `a=1`, because `r` is selected before taking the near-Einstein sequence limit.  If `K_0` varies along a family, the choice of `r` and the resulting `r^{-2}` bound must be uniform for that family.

The velocity estimate gives bilipschitz metric displacement:

\[
\int_0^T|aE|\,dt\le C\delta r^2.
\tag{6.3}
\]

It does not imply curvature at time `T` is close to curvature at time `0`; curvature contains second spatial derivatives.  The initial hypotheses do not provide pointwise transition curvature bounds.  The intended contradiction uses bounded curvature on plateau buffers plus exponential-pullback averaging; it does not need pointwise transition curvature closeness.

## 7. Unweighted defect remains separate

The global recalibration needs unweighted defect energy

\[
Q_\alpha(t)=\int\eta_\alpha^2|E|^2.
\]

The required structure is triangular:

\[
Q_\alpha'(t)
\le Cr^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}Q_\beta(t),
\tag{7.1}
\]

with no curvature-only additive source such as `epsilon int a|nabla Rm|^2`.  Homogeneity of the flow at `E=0` makes this plausible, but it still requires an exact tensor calculation with evolving measure, cutoffs, and Hessian-`a` integrations by parts.

## 8. Current analytic tasks

The corrected smoothing route now has these distinct tasks:

1. prove the exact tensor `q=2` inequality and the graph absorption leading to (4.3)--(4.6);
2. derive the graph-semigroup cubic potential (5.4);
3. prove the weak nested time-space estimate for `H_q` and `J_m` with correct inner/outer cutoffs;
4. prove positive-time persistence of a fixed defect moment, especially `J_6`, without integrating a nonintegrable `1/t` coefficient from zero;
5. prove the triangular unweighted `Q` estimate (7.1);
6. use plateau bounded curvature over a short time interval, not just a single terminal value, to obtain the controlled exponential-pullback charts needed for the calibrated Derdzinski contradiction.

These would strengthen only the critical four-dimensional negative LeBrun/Ishida--LeBrun route.  The positive branch, arbitrary four-dimensional no-Einstein manifolds, dimensions `n>=5`, the original all-dimensional proposition, and Lean formalization remain unsolved.

## Files

- Normalization computation: `workspace/scripts/step22_energy_normalization.py`
- Graph bookkeeping: `workspace/scripts/step22_first_exit_energy.py`
- Weak-moment ledger: `workspace/scripts/step22_weak_moment_ledger.py`
- This note: `workspace/notes/step22_current_energy_formulation.md`
- Companion weak estimate: `workspace/notes/step22_weak_nested_moment_estimate.md`

## 9. Defect-moment stability ledger

A final algebra check was added in `workspace/scripts/step22_defect_Q_j6_ledger.py`.
For fixed weighted defect moments

\[
J_m=\int\eta^2a^{m-2}|E|^m,
\qquad z_m=\eta a^{(m-1)/2}|E|^{m/2},
\]

the curvature reaction is exactly

\[
\int Fz_m^2.
\]

Thus a fixed exponent such as `m=6` can be controlled directly by the current critical product `gamma=A^2||F||_2`, giving a term of the form

\[
\Gamma_*(X_m+r^{-2}J_m),
\]

rather than by integrating the positive-time cubic potential `H_3(s)~1/s` from zero.  This is the right starting point before applying the later `m -> 3m/2` product.

For the unweighted defect energy

\[
Q=\int\eta^2|E|^2,
\]

the curvature potential has the monomial form

\[
\int\eta^2aF|E|^2=\int Fw^2,
\qquad w=\eta a^{1/2}E.
\]

Sobolev on `w` produces `a|nabla E|^2`, `|da|^2/a |E|^2`, and cutoff remainders, all still multiplied by `E`; no curvature-only monomial appears at this algebraic level.  This supports, but does not prove, the triangular `Q` estimate in Section 7; the exact tensor evolution must still be written.
